To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) small particles of tin and lead have melting points below their macroscopic melting points, (2) the smaller the particles, the lower the melting point, and (3) the melting points of the small particles are independent of the method used to produce them (evaporation, precipitation, or condensation).

the melting point of particles with diameters in the range 20 to 200 nm is lower than that of bulk material by 0.5° to 1° C per 10 nm decrease in diameter, and that the effect is not due to a change in the melting temperature of the bulk solid, but rather to the melting of the solid particles at a temperature lower than that of their bulk solid.
the melting of a very small particle (radius of 10 nm or less) is a two-step process: first, the particle is heated to its melting point, and then it is melted.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the melting point depression of small particles of lead.
the effect of size and shape on the melting of very small particles.
the melting of very small solid particles during evaporation at constant temperature.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, for a particle diameter of less than about 20 nm, the melting point is depressed by an amount proportional to the reciprocal of the particle diameter, and the proportionality constant is the same for all materials.

the melting point of a solid particle of diameter D is given by T _{D}  = T _{0} (1 − kD) where T _{0} is the melting point of the bulk solid, k is a constant of the order of 10 ^{−3}, and D is expressed in nm.
the melting point is depressed by about 10 per cent when the particle radius is reduced from 100 nm to about 20 nm, and that the effect becomes more marked as the particle size is reduced further.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the melting point of particles of a few nanometres diameter is depressed by a few hundred degrees, and that the depression is proportional to 1/r, where r is the radius of the particle.
the melting point depression is a function of particle diameter, and that it is not possible to define a single melting point for a material when it exists in the form of particles of different size.
the melting point of particles of diameter 20 nm is about 50 °C lower than that of bulk metal.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the melting point of a nanoparticle is not the same as that of the bulk, and the difference can be significant.
the melting point of a small particle is not simply a function of its size, as is the case with larger particles, but is also a function of the particle’s shape and its surface energy.
the size of the particles is not the main factor in the melting process.
